kp.k: Record funding coincided with substantially fewer deals
kp.d: Richard Tromans reports Legal Complex data showing that 2024 legal tech funding exceeded every year going back to 2015, while deal numbers fell to 356 from the 2021 peak of 575. The coverage uses a broad definition of businesses with a legal process at their core, rather than a narrowly defined legal software market.
qs: companies that utilize a legal process at the core of their business model
was higher than in any year going back to 2015.
Also, the total number of deals is down a lot, to 356, compared to 575 at the peak of deal volume back in 2021.

kp.k: Debt became the largest funding segment
kp.d: The article reports more than $5 billion in debt finance in 2024, making debt the largest funding segment by value despite high interest rates. Fewer companies took debt than in 2023; Tromans interprets this as suggesting that some larger companies borrowed disproportionately large amounts, rather than documenting their individual borrowing.
qs: Debt is now the top segment for funding legal tech in terms of total value.
In fact, it’s now at over $5 billion in 2024.
And this is at a time of very high interest rates as well.
which suggests some larger companies are taking on a lot more than everyone else.

kp.k: Capital concentration suggests a maturing legal technology market
kp.d: Tromans attributes higher funding alongside fewer deals to larger companies absorbing substantial fresh capital, even as new generative-AI companies launched since 2023 grow. He cites Harvey's $100m raise in 2024 as an example of startup funding and Dye & Durham as an example of significant funding for a larger company, interpreting the latter as evidence of sustained investor appetite for established, scaled businesses.
qs: much larger companies are soaking up a huge amount of the fresh capital.
This is simply a sign of a maturing legal tech market, even as a whole range of new genAI-based companies have arrived since 2023 and are now on a growth surge.
Harvey for example bagged $100m last year.
At the same time some larger companies bagged significant funding, sometimes ones that don’t always hit the newsstands, such as Dye & Durham.

kp.k: Funding bifurcation may disadvantage older, unscaled companies
kp.d: Tromans explicitly offers a theory, not an established finding, that investors increasingly favour either very young startups promising rapid growth or large companies with proven scale. Companies dating from the legal tech boom around 2016 that have not scaled substantially may consequently attract less interest. This proposed bifurcation explains the apparent paradox of fewer deals despite generative AI prompting new startup formation.
qs: One potential reason is that **money is bifurcating** between the very new startups that are just a couple of years old and promise rapid growth, and the very large scaled-up companies that are seen as a sure bet and have proven themselves already.

Meanwhile, it’s possible that some companies that have been around for some years since the first wave of the legal tech boom in 2016, but have not scaled considerably since then, are seeing less interest from investors – but that’s just AL’s theory as to why we have a record year for funding, but far fewer deals.

kp.k: Generative AI could renew incumbents' growth opportunities
kp.d: Tromans argues that older legal AI companies can also adopt generative AI and may now encounter market conditions conducive to substantial growth. He presents this as a conditional opportunity dependent on investor support and market perceptions, not a demonstrated outcome, and recommends investment consideration across the full spectrum of legal tech companies rather than treating past limited growth as determinative.
qs: A first-generation legal AI company from 2016 can provide genAI capabilities as well.
The challenge, as ever, is the story they tell to the market and how they are perceived by potential investors.
An early mover from 2016 may in fact now finally be seeing the right conditions for massive growth – if only investors would get behind them and support their scaling.

In short, investors should be looking at the whole spectrum of legal tech companies for investment opportunities, as all such companies have an opportunity for greater growth as the legal tech market expands in general on a global basis.

kp.k: Debt may reflect viability and heightened competitive capital needs
kp.d: Legal Complex founder Raymond Blyd offers two interpretations of debt financing: continued private-equity and bank confidence in mature legal tech companies, and those companies' increased capital requirements to compete. He speculates that competition from Microsoft, OpenAI, Adobe and Box, alongside well-capitalized AI-native startups, may explain the latter.
qs: Debt can be viewed in two ways. First, Private Equity and banks still view mature legal tech companies as viable investments.

Second, mature companies need way more capital to compete in the current legal tech market. Perhaps this is because of the incursion by bigger companies like Microsoft, OpenAI, Adobe, and Box. As well as the aggressive competition by AI-native well-capitalized startups.

kp.k: AI funding patterns warrant attention without explaining all investment
kp.d: Blyd observes that AI companies raised more often, while cautioning through his initial reaction that not every new 2024 investment targeted AI. Looking ahead, he identifies 2025 M&A as worth watching, particularly companies that raised between 2020–2022 but could not raise in 2023–2024; this is an outlook rather than a reported acquisition outcome.
qs: My initial reaction to the 2024 numbers was that not every new investment was aimed at AI.

The M&A space will be very interesting to watch in 2025. Especially, the companies that were able to raise between 2020 – 2022 and weren’t able to raise in 2023 – 2024. I also noticed that AI companies raised more often.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Tromans argues that genAI is driving legal-tech startup formation and market growth, while suggesting that investment is concentrating at the newest and largest ends of the market. Blyd suggests that AI-related competition may be increasing mature companies' capital requirements.
pts.d: Richard Tromans says genAI has prompted new startups and changed legal-market expectations, potentially creating renewed growth opportunities for older legal-tech companies as well. He presents funding bifurcation between young, fast-growth startups and large, established companies as a theory, not an established finding. Older companies that have not scaled substantially may be attracting less investor interest, but can also adopt genAI and potentially grow with investor support. Legal Complex founder Raymond Blyd says mature legal-tech companies need more capital to compete, potentially because of large technology companies and well-capitalized AI-native startups. Blyd also reports that AI companies raised funding more often and flags 2025 M&A activity for attention, without predicting specific transactions. These are claims about legal-tech markets and financing, not demonstrated changes in lawyers' productivity or employment.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source combines Legal Complex funding data, funding examples, Tromans's explicitly qualified interpretation, and Blyd's industry observations.
pts.d: Legal Complex's data indicate that 2024 funding was the highest in the series going back to 2015, debt exceeded $5 billion, and deal volume was 356 versus 575 at the 2021 peak. The dataset uses a broad definition of legal tech: companies with a legal process at the core of their business model. Tromans cites Harvey's $100 million raise and significant funding for Dye & Durham as examples. These figures establish the financing context; the source does not offer a quantitative causal test connecting genAI to funding concentration or growth. Tromans expressly labels reduced interest in older, insufficiently scaled companies as his theory. Blyd invokes more than ten years following the sector and says he noticed AI companies raising more often, but provides no numerical comparison for that observation. He also cautions that not every investment targeted AI.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The analysis concerns 2024 financing, the genAI startup wave since 2023, conditional growth opportunities for older firms, and a 2025 M&A outlook.
pts.d: Writing in 2025, Tromans compares 2024 funding with the series since 2015 and deal volume with the 2021 peak. He places the new genAI-company wave since 2023 and discusses companies dating from the 2016 legal-tech boom. Renewed growth for older providers is a possibility rather than a dated forecast: access to genAI alone is not sufficient, since investor perceptions, market positioning, and support for scaling matter. Blyd's competitive explanation is qualified by 'Perhaps.' His 2025 M&A watch focuses particularly on companies that raised during 2020–2022 but could not raise during 2023–2024.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected groups are legal-tech startups, mature providers, older companies that have not scaled, and their investors and lenders.
pts.d: Tromans portrays young genAI startups as attracting investment through growth prospects and large scaled providers as attracting capital through perceived stability. Older, incompletely scaled companies may be overlooked but could use genAI to pursue renewed growth. He urges investors to consider the full spectrum of providers. Blyd identifies mature legal-tech businesses as facing larger capital needs amid competition from major technology companies and well-funded AI-native startups, while private equity and banks continue to view mature providers as viable investments. The article does not identify concrete consequences for particular lawyer roles, law-firm staffing structures, clients, or access to justice.
